page.metaLead: A 4-day wildlife photography workshop in Panna, Madhya Pradesh, with 5 safaris and in-field guidance.
page.heroLine: 3 nights / 4 days · 5 safaris · Limited seats · Price on enquiry (single room)
intro: Four days in one of central India's quietest tiger reserves, built entirely around making photographs. Mornings and evenings in the field, breakfast in the bush, and unhurried evening sessions where we go through the day's frames together. Kept deliberately small, so the guidance is personal and the jeeps never crowded.

This is a workshop, not a sightseeing tour. The aim is to send you home with images you're proud of, and with the habits that made them: reading light, anticipating behaviour, choosing your position before the moment arrives.
why: Panna Tiger Reserve sits in Madhya Pradesh, a short drive from the temple town of Khajuraho. It's one of Indian conservation's great comeback stories: tigers were lost here around 2009 and carefully reintroduced, and the reserve has since recovered into a thriving habitat. I've written [the full story of Panna's tiger recovery](/blog/the-panna-story) in the journal. The Ken river runs through it, cutting gorges and plateaus that give the landscape a character quite different from the more famous reserves. Beyond tigers, Panna is rich in leopards, sloth bears, crocodiles along the Ken, and some of central India's best raptor and vulture activity.

The departures run through Panna's dry, cool season, from the fresh, green forest just after the monsoon to the crisp heart of winter, when misty mornings and a drying forest draw wildlife to the Ken. Soft light, comfortable temperatures, and a quiet, uncrowded park. It's a beautiful time to photograph it.
howTheDaysRun: Out before first light for the morning safari, with breakfast carried into the bush so we stay in the field through the best light. Back to the lodge for lunch and a quiet middle of the day. Out again for the evening safari as the light turns. After dinner, a photography and post-processing session: looking at what came home, talking through what worked, and building the edit. The trip opens with an evening safari on arrival day. On the last day, we have breakfast at the lodge before departure. That makes five safaris across the trip.

page.metaLead: A 5-day wildlife photography workshop in Corbett Tiger Reserve, Uttarakhand, with 6 safaris from Dhikala.
page.heroLine: 4 nights / 5 days · 6 safaris · Accommodation in the core zone · Limited seats · Price on enquiry (twin sharing)
intro: This is a 5-day wildlife photography workshop in Corbett Tiger Reserve, in the state of Uttarakhand. We start and end the trip in Delhi. We stay 3 nights at the government Forest Rest House in Dhikala. Dhikala is in the core zone, the most protected part of the reserve. We go on 6 safaris across the trip. The group is small, so I can give each guest personal help in the field.

The workshop is for anyone who wants to make better wildlife photographs. You do not need experience. In the jeep, I help you read the light and set your camera. Each evening, we look at your photographs together. We talk about what worked and what to try next. I also teach post-processing, which means editing your photographs on a computer. You go home with better photographs and the habits that helped you make them.
why: Corbett Tiger Reserve covers about 1,288 sq km. At its centre is the national park, of about 521 sq km. This is the core zone. The forest around the core is the buffer zone, where some human use is allowed. The park opened in 1936 as Hailey National Park. It was the first national park in mainland Asia. Today it has the name of Jim Corbett, a hunter who became a naturalist and author. In 1973, Corbett became one of the first nine reserves of Project Tiger, the national programme to protect tigers. The 2022 national tiger count recorded 260 tigers here. No other Indian tiger reserve recorded more.

Most of the park is dense forest of sal, a tall tree. Sal and many other trees here are deciduous, which means they lose their leaves in the dry season. Open grasslands cover about 10% of the park. Local people call these grasslands "chaur". The Ramganga River runs through the park. It has gharials, mugger crocodiles and otters. A gharial is a fish-eating crocodile with a long, thin snout. Other mammals include leopard, Asian elephant, sloth bear and several types of deer. The park also has records of more than 580 bird species. The departures run in March. When the deciduous trees lose their leaves, you can see further into the forest.
howTheDaysRun: On the first day, we drive from Delhi to Ramnagar, at the edge of Corbett. The next morning, we drive into Dhikala, and we go on our first safari that evening. On the two full days in Dhikala, we go on a morning safari and an evening safari. Each evening in Corbett, we review your photographs and work on post-processing together. On the last day, we go on one more morning safari. Then we drive back to Delhi. That makes 6 safaris across the trip.

page.metaLead: A 5-day wildlife photography workshop in Kanha, Madhya Pradesh, with 6 safaris and just 3 guests.
page.heroLine: 4 nights / 5 days · 6 safaris · Up to 3 guests · Single room (twin sharing on request)
intro: Five days in Kanha Tiger Reserve, all about one thing: making better wildlife photographs. You fly into Nagpur, and I take care of the drive to Kanha and back. We stay four nights, and your room and all your meals are covered. Over the trip, we go on six safaris, which are drives through the park to find and photograph wildlife. There are only three guests, so I can work with each of you in the field.

You don't need any experience. Out on safari, I'll help you read the light and pick your camera settings. In the evenings, we go through your photographs together and talk about what worked and what to try next. I'll help you with the post-processing of your images, turning your RAW files into frames you'll cherish for a long time. By the end of the trip, you'll have stronger images and a process you can repeat on your own.
why: Kanha has been guarded for almost a century. It became a wildlife sanctuary in 1933 and a national park in 1955. In 1973, it was one of the first nine reserves of Project Tiger, India's programme to save its tigers. Today its core holds 917 sq km of tall sal forest, bamboo hills and wide grass meadows in the Mandla district of Madhya Pradesh. A buffer zone of 1,134 sq km surrounds it, where people live and work at the edge of the wild.

The meadows hold Kanha's greatest comeback. The hard-ground barasingha, a swamp deer and the state animal of Madhya Pradesh, lives in the wild here and nowhere else. In 1967, only 66 were left. Today there are about 1,100. Barasingha, other deer and gaur, the Indian bison, graze out in the open, so you get room to work and a clear line of sight. The tiger, the leopard, the sloth bear and the dhole, India's wild dog, move through the same forest. And overhead, there are about 300 species of birds.
We go in February, in the dry season. The trees on the hills drop their leaves, and the forest opens up. Light reaches deeper into the trees, and so does your view.
howTheDaysRun: On Day 1, you land in Nagpur and we drive to Kanha together. We check in at the lodge in the afternoon, chat about Kanha and its history, and get your camera set up. Then we meet at 8:00 pm for a briefing and dinner.

Days 2–4 are the full workshop days. We wake up at 5:30 am and head out on the morning safari at 6:00 am, with breakfast packed to eat in the forest. We're back at the lodge by 11:30 am for lunch. The evening safari starts at 3:00 pm, and we get back around 7:00 pm. At 8:00 pm, we sit down together to go through the day's photographs and edit them. Dinner is at 9:00 pm. That's two safaris a day, six in all.
On Day 5, we have breakfast, check out, and leave for Nagpur Airport at 11:30 am.
